sentences.text:
Learned Sr.
Advocate appearing for the Petitioners submits that even otherwise, his clients are entitled to have the land & the structures built thereon retained under the 'Akrama Sakrama' Scheme.

2. After service of notice, the State has entered appearance through the learned AGA; the BDA and its SLAO are represented by their Sr. Panel Counsel who has filed the Statement of Objections dated 15.01.2021 resisting the Writ Petition.
Learned Panel Counsel makes passionate submission justifying the acquisition in question.

3. Having heard the learned counsel for the parties and having perused the Petition papers, this Court declines indulgence in the matter for the following reasons:
(a) The Preliminary Notification was issued on 21.03.1977 inter alia comprising the petition land for the formation of a layout.
The Final Notification came to be issued on 14.05.1980; the award came to be passed on 09.11.1982.

The Award Notice dated 05.12.1982 was sent to the Khathedars namely Govinda, Munishamappa & Nagappa under Section 12(2) of the erstwhile Land Acquisition Act, 1894 and the same was served on them on 08.12.1982.
The possession of the property was taken on 14.12.1982 by drawing the mahazar which bears the signatures of a few residents of the area.
The name of BDA came to be entered in the Revenue Records vide MR No.1/1990-91.
The Writ Petition is filed on 23.09.2020 with no plausible explanation for a long & inordinate delay of about four decades or so.

The Apex Court in MUNICIPAL COUNCIL AHMEDNAGAR v SHAH HYDER BEIG, 2000 (2) SCC 48, at paragraph 14 has observed as under:
"...While it is true that this extraordinary jurisdiction is available to mitigate the sufferings of the people in general but it is not out of place to mention that this extraordinary jurisdiction, has been conferred on to the law courts under Article 226 of the Constitution on a very sound equitable principle,

entities.text: MUNICIPAL COUNCIL AHMEDNAGAR v SHAH HYDER BEIG, 2000 (2) SCC 48
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Hence, the equitable doctrine, namely, delay defects equity has its fullest application in the matter of grant of relief under Article 226 of the Constitution.
The discretionary relief can be had provided one has not by his act or conduct given a go-bye to his rights.

Equity favours a vigilant rather than an indolent litigant and this being the basic tenet of law, the question of grant of an order as has been passed in the matter as regards restoration of possession upon cancellation of the notification does not and cannot arise..."

(b) The submission of learned Sr. Advocate, Me. Mohate appearing for the Petitioners that the Scheme having not been executed within the prescribed statutory period, the same has lapsed and as a consequence, the acquisition itself needs to be voided, is bit difficult to countenance.
A wealth of material is produced by the BDA to prima facie show that the acquisition having been accomplished

even the possession of the property was taken over on 14.12.1982 itself by drawing the mahazar.
However, Petitioners had filed an injunctive suit in O.S.No.4415/2020 and secured a status quo order on 25.09.2020.
With the aid of this order, Petitioners wanted to protect the structure in question.
No material is produced to show that this structure was put up before the issuance of Preliminary Notification.

Neither the Building Plan, nor the Building License, nor the particulars of power & water supply installations, nor the 1st payment of tax, nor the particulars availment of telephone facility, etc have been pleaded much less furnished.
That being the position, the version of the Petitioners that they have been in the settled possession of the subject property cannot be countenanced.

The vehement submission of learned Sr. counsel for the Petitioners that in the absence of a Notification issued under Section 16(2) of 1894 Act, the taking of possession cannot be assumed does not merit acceptance vide a Full Bench decision of this Court in ITI EMPLOYEES HOUSING COOEPRATIVE SOCIETY LTD., vs. VENKATAPPA, 2010 4 KLJ 19.

entities.text: ITI EMPLOYEES HOUSING COOEPRATIVE SOCIETY LTD., vs. VENKATAPPA, 2010 4 KLJ 19
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Once there is such a 16(2) Notification, it would be almost conclusive evidence of taking possession; however, from this it does not follow that by no other evidentiary material, taking of possession can be established.

(c) The vehement contention advanced on behalf of the Petitioners that no notice was sent to the land owners asking them to give up the possession and therefore, by merely drawing the mahazar one cannot presume that the possession has been taken over from the land owners, cannot be agreed to.
The manner of taking possession is not prescribed either under the 1894 Act or under the 1976 Act.

The possession of immovable property has to be taken in a manner admissible to the nature of property; there can be no hard and fast rules laying down as to what act would be sufficient to constitute taking of possession.

The Full Bench of this Court in ITI EMPLOYEES, supra at paragraph 20 had observed as under:
"...One of the accepted modes of taking possession of the acquired land is recording of a memorandum or a panchanama by the Deputy Commissioner (or the Land Acquisition Officer) in the presence of witnesses signed by them and that would constitute taking possession of the land as it is impossible to take physical possession of the acquired land.

The presence of the owner or the occupant of the land is not necessary to effectuate the taking of possession as it is common knowledge that invariably in most of the cases, the owner or occupier of the land may not co-operate in taking possession of the land.
It is also strictly not necessary as a matter of fact or legal requirement that notice should be given to the owner or occupant of the land that possession would be taken at a particular time.

The fact of such taking possession may be notified by the Deputy Commissioner (or the Land Acquisition Officer) in the Official Gazette as envisaged under Section 16(2) of the Act and such notification shall be evidence of fact of taking such possession for the vesting of the land in the State Government.

Under Section 16, the Deputy Commissioner has been authorised to take possession of land regarding which an award has been made by him under Section 11 and thereupon, the land shall vest in the Government free of all encumbrances..."

It hardly needs to be stated after the land has vested in the State by virtue of passing of the Award and taking of possession, one who claims to be in occupation of the property is no less than a Smt.B.L.Ramadevi vs The State Of Karnataka on 13 February, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/93827471/
4 trespasser.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Apex Court in INDORE DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY vs. MAHOHAR LAL, 2020 (8) SCC 129, paragraph 345 has observed "...once panchanama had been drawn of taking possession, thereafter re-entry or retaining the possession is that of the trespasser..."

entities.text: INDORE DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY vs. MAHOHAR LAL, 2020 (8) SCC 129
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: (d) The next submission of learned Sr. Advocate, Mr. Mohate that the Scheme having not been executed in time, the acquisition has lapsed both under Section 27 of the 1976 Act and under Section 24(2) of 2013 Act does not impress the Court, and reasons for this are not far to seek:

In order to invoke lapsing of the Scheme under Section 27, there are three pre-conditions, namely: (i) there must be failure to execute the Scheme because of dereliction of statutory duties on the part of the officials sans justification; (ii) a mere delay in substantial execution of the Scheme would not do;
(iii) the challenge on the ground of lapse of Scheme should be without brooking delay, vide Division Bench decision in KRISHNAMURTHY vs. BANGALORE DEVELOPMENT - 10 - AUTHORITY, ILR 1996 KAR 1258.

entities.text: KRISHNAMURTHY vs. BANGALORE DEVELOPMENT - 10 - AUTHORITY, ILR 1996 KAR 1258
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Petitioners have not laid any foundation in their pleadings with regard to the same and much less placed any material to substantiate the said claim of lapsing.

Coming to the lapse of acquisition under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act, firstly, this Act would not apply to acquisitions done under the statutes other than 1894 Act, there being sufficient regulatory provisions in the 1976 Act itself vide the Division Bench decision in W.A.No.1415/2018 (LA-BDA)
between SRI. L. RAMAREDDY v. STATE & OTHERS, disposed off on 01.05.2020, vide paragraph 20.
This apart, what the Apex Court observed in INDORE DEVELOPMENT supra at paragraph 345 & 346 is very relevant.

It reads as under:
"...Section 24(2) is sought to be used as an umbrella so as to question the concluded proceedings in which possession has been taken, development has been made, and compensation has been deposited, but may be due to refusal, it has not been collected.

The challenge to the acquisition proceedings cannot be made within the parameters of Section 24(2) once panchnama had been drawn of taking possession,
thereafter re-entry or retaining the possession is that of the trespasser.
The legality of the proceedings cannot be challenged belatedly, and the right to challenge cannot be revived by virtue of the - 11 - provisions of Section 24(2).
Section 24(2) only contemplates lethargy/inaction of the authorities to act for five years or more.
It is very easy to lay a claim that physical possession was not taken, with respect to open land.

Yet, once vesting takes place,
possession is presumed to be that of the owner, i.e., the State Government and land has been transferred to the beneficiaries, Corporations, Authorities, etc., for developmental purposes and third-party interests have intervened.
Such challenges cannot be entertained at all under the purview of Section 24(2) as it is not what is remotely contemplated in Section 24(2) of the Act of 2013.

sentences.text: 5 In matters of land acquisition, this Court has frowned upon, and cautioned courts about delays and held that delay is fatal in questioning the land acquisition proceedings.

In case possession has not been taken in accordance with law and vesting is not in accordance with Section 16, proceedings before courts are to be initiated within reasonable time, not after the lapse of several decades..."

(e) The next submission of learned Sr. Advocate for the Petitioners that in respect of certain lands,
almost adjoining Petitioners' the acquisition has been waived or given up and therefore, on the principle of parity Petitioners should also be given the same benefit, is bit difficult to agree with.

Where the Scheme has not been substantially executed despite all possibilities of execution,
- 12 - only then one can assume that the Scheme has lapsed and therefore, the land which has not vested in the State can be given back to its owner.

The Apex Court in OFFSHORE HOLDINGS Vs BANGALORE DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY, (2011) 3 SCC 139, at paragraph 38 has observed as under:
"...On a conjunctive reading of the provisions of Sections 27 and 36 of the State Act, it is clear that where a scheme lapses, the acquisition may not.

entities.text: OFFSHORE HOLDINGS Vs BANGALORE DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY, (2011) 3 SCC 139
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: This, of course, will depend upon the facts and circumstances of a given case.

Where, upon completion of the acquisition proceedings, the land has vested in the State Government in terms of Section 16 of the Land Acquisition Act, the acquisition would not lapse or terminate as a result of lapsing of the scheme under Section 27 of the BDA Act.

An argument to the contrary cannot be accepted for the reason that on vesting, the land stands transferred and vested in the State/Authority free from all encumbrances and such status of the property is incapable of being altered by fiction of law either by the State Act or by the Central Act.
Both these Acts do not contain any provision in terms of which property, once and absolutely, vested in the State can be reverted to the owner on any condition.
There is no reversal of the title and possession of the State.

However, this may not be true in cases where acquisition proceedings are still pending and land has not been vested in the Government in terms of Section 16 of the Land Acquisition Act..."
- 13 - (f) The submission made on behalf of the Petitioners that the payment of compensation to the land owners, is a pre-condition for sustaining the acquisition proceedings does not merit acceptance.
True it is, that the Right to Property is constitutionally guaranteed under Article 300A.
Under the Scheme envisaged in the 1976 Act, the land will vest in the State once the Award has been passed and possession thereof has been taken.
Non- payment of compensation per se does not vitiate the acquisition, subject to all just exceptions into which argued case of the Petitioners does not fit.

This view gains support from the Division Bench decision in W.A.no.4121/2017 (LA-BDA) between the BANGALORE DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY vs. PRINCIPAL SECRETARY, disposed off on Smt.B.L.Ramadevi vs The State Of Karnataka on 13 February, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/93827471/
6 24.05.2022, as rightly contended by learned Sr. Panel Counsel appearing for the Authority.

entities.text: BANGALORE DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY vs. PRINCIPAL SECRETARY
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Smt.B.L.Ramadevi vs The State Of Karnataka
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is not that no Award Notice was sent to the Khatedars.
In fact, the Award Notice dated 05.12.1982 was served on the original Khatedars on 08.12.1982.
It is open to the - 14 - true owners of the land to seek compensation in terms of the Award, since the same is said to be in Revenue Deposit.

(g) There is a lot of force in the passionate submission of learned Panel Counsel appearing for the BDA that the Petitioners have suppressed about the earlier rounds of litigation taken up by the Khatedars of subject land.
Their first challenge in W.P.No.15383/1983 was dismissed by a Coordinate Bench of this Court.
A second challenge was laid in W.P.No.11585/1985 and that too met the same fate.
Further, the W.A. No.1494/1986 was also dismissed by the Division Bench.
When confronted as to why this has not been disclosed in the Petition, there is absolutely no explanation whatsoever.
It has been a settled position of law that Writ remedy is equitable and those who seek refuge in Writ Jurisdiction should lay himself bare.
A litigant has to approach the Court with clean hands, clean head and clean heart.
Those who are - 15 - not clean in this way cannot be permitted to bell the temple of justice.

(h) It is stated by the learned Sr. Advocate appearing for the Petitioners that a huge school building (about 2000 sq. ft) exists in the subject property and if the same is taken away now, the school children, teachers & other employees would be put to a great hardship & manifest injustice.

Learned Sr. Panel Counsel appearing for the Respondent - BDA, in his usual fairness answers that some reasonable period may be fixed by this Court on the expiry of which the Petitioners should peaceably quit the property on their own.
This matter involves competing equities which the Court has to balance taking into consideration the interest of all the stakeholders, more particularly, the teachers & the taught.
Decades have rolled in this legal battle and admittedly, the school building exists since some years.
Asking the Petitioners to quit the same at once, would do a manifest injustice not only to them but also to the students.

Regard being had to - 16 - all the relevant factors, this Court is of a considered opinion that justice of the case warrants granting of a period of two years to quit the premises provided that the Petitioners file an undertaking by way of affidavit to that effect.
